title: Three acts commonly: knowledge, assent, and fiducia applying the promise
source_text: XXVII. Quod attinet ad fidei actus, Reformati plurimi tres fidei justificantis actus, sive partes distinguere solent. Primus est notitia qua verbum Dei, saltem secundum ea quae sunt ad salutem scitu necessaria, cognoscimus & intelligimus. Secundus est assensus quem praebemus omnibus illis quae verbo Dei revelata sunt. Tertius est fiducia qua credens generale promissionis verbum specialiter sibi applicat. Haec est doctrina Ursini & Paraei in Explicationibus Catecheticis, quaestione 21. Wendelini Christianae Theologiae lib. 2. cap. 24. Thesi 14, & 15. Tileni disputatione de fide justificante, Thesi 20. & Trelcatii quoque, loco supra citato.
pass_a_gloss: As for the acts of faith, most of the Reformed are wont to distinguish three acts, or parts, of justifying faith. The first is knowledge by which we know and understand the word of God, at least according to those things which are necessary to be known unto salvation. The second is the assent which we give to all those things which have been revealed by the word of God. The third is trust by which the believer specially applies to himself the general word of promise. This is the doctrine of Ursinus and Paraeus in the Catechetical Explications, question 21; of Wendelin in Christian Theology book 2, chapter 24, Theses 14 and 15; of Tilenus in the disputation on justifying faith, Thesis 20; and of Trelcatius also, in the place cited above.
pass_b_english: Most Reformed: three acts/parts of justifying faith.
1. Notitia — know God’s word at least as needed for salvation.
2. Assensus — assent to all God revealed.
3. Fiducia — believer specially applies the general promise-word to himself.
Ursinus/Paraeus Cat. Expl. 21; Wendelin; Tilenus; Trelcatius.
